title: Quick Reference: One Sprint at a Glance
body: ## Quick Reference: One Sprint at a Glance This is the **one-page operational companion** to the full manual. Use it during a work session instead of reading the entire wiki repeatedly. ### When to use Use it when deciding what prompt to run next, which file the agent should update, what you must personally approve and when to stop. ### Current state → next action | Status in `STATE.md` | Agent action | Human action | | --- | --- | --- | | `discovering` | Summarize known/unknown; ask one question | Choose concept or request options | | `designing` | Propose one slice, research, tradeoffs and `AC-##` | Decide meaningful direction (Gate D) | | `awaiting_approval` | Show exact `PLAN.md` revision, paths, commands and risks | Explicitly authorize or revise (Gate I) | | `implementing` | Change **only** approved source and log evidence | Review deviations if any | | `refining` | Diagnose observed defect; check existing authorization | Choose correction or approve revised scope | | `awaiting_acceptance` | Provide tested artifact, limitations and playtest steps | Play/review and provide Gate A | | `accepted` | Preserve verdict, retro and backlog handoff | Choose next sprint if desired | | `rejected` | Preserve rejection; propose safe direction | Decide revise/abandon | | `paused` | Record blocker, last safe state and resume requirements | Supply needed authorization or context | **The stage** is a separate field: research/design/implement/refine/acceptance. Status and stage must agree with the workflow contract. ### Files you will see ```text AGENTS.md agent conduct / role boundaries SECURITY.md prohibited reads, tools, external effects GAME.md chosen player experience and constraints STATE.md current verified status, next action, gates DECISIONS.md actual material human choices planning/BACKLOG.md candidates and deferred ideas planning/sprints/sprint-NNN/ SPRINT.md goal, tradeoffs, acceptance criteria, Gate D PLAN.md dry run, operations, commands, Gate I REVIEW.md real results, playtest and Gate A ``` ### The three questions to ask before authorizing work **Design:** Is the player action/outcome clear, and do I actually choose this approach? **Implementation:** Have I seen *exactly* which files/commands/dependencies/side effects this plan revision permits? **Acceptance:** Have I actually played or inspected the result and reported my verdict, rather than trusting a green test? ### A quick “stop” checklist Stop before edits if: - the current plan revision isn't explicitly authorized by you; - a new path, dependency, command, paid service, privacy risk or deployment is needed; - the worktree/source state conflicts with the plan; - the assistant claims an approval you cannot verify; - a human review has not occurred but status says `accepted`. ### Commands To check your own project file structure from the Light framework repository: ```bash python3 scripts/validate_light.py /path/to/your-game ``` To check the distributed unstarted starter kit: ```bash python3 scripts/validate_light.py starter-kit/minimal --mode template --sprint-template starter-kit/sprint-template ``` A PASS means **structural consistency only**, not authenticated human consent. ### Common failures **Blind prompt chaining:** Automatically run START→IMPLEMENT. Pick prompt based on verified state and stop at each human gate. **Routine overload:** Require permission for trivial variable names. Let agents choose T0 details within scope. ### Related [Quick Start in repo](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/QUICK_START.md) · [Prompt catalog](#wiki-reference--prompt-catalog) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals)

title: The Five-Stage Game Development Lifecycle
body: ## The Five-Stage Game Development Lifecycle Every ADDF Light Games sprint works toward a **small, verifiable player-facing outcome**. The five stages are Research → Design / Ideation → Implement → Refine → Acceptance. They describe what the user experiences, while Research/Design/Develop *capabilities* determine which files an agent may write. ### When to use Read when starting a sprint, training an agent, deciding a next prompt, or reconciling a status that doesn't match the current work. ### Lifecycle map | Stage | Primary question | Persistent work | Exit | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Research** | What don't we yet know, and why does it matter? | Evidence, questions, game hypothesis | Enough information to propose an experiment/decision | | **Design / Ideation** | What exact player behavior and test will this sprint target? | `SPRINT.md`, decisions, criteria, learning checkpoint | Human Gate D resolved or validly not required | | **Implement** | What exact files and commands may be changed? | Approved `PLAN.md`, code/tests/assets, execution record | Report actual evidence or a blocker | | **Refine** | What did the test/playtest reveal and what should change? | `REVIEW.md` rounds, bounded corrections, revised plan if needed | Retest ready or ask for new scope approval | | **Acceptance** | Does the real outcome meet the human's expectations? | Criterion results, human verdict, retrospective | Human Gate A, or return to refinement/rejection/pause | A sprint can loop from refinement to design when the intended experience changes. The workflow is not a waterfall of huge milestones. ### Status is not the same as stage `STATE.md` also records one **sprint status**: `discovering`, `designing`, `awaiting_approval`, `implementing`, `refining`, `awaiting_acceptance`, `accepted`, `rejected`, `paused`. For example, `awaiting_approval` is a *status* during Design while the human evaluates a technical plan. Formal allowed transitions and paused-state recovery are defined in the normative [Workflow States specification](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/WORKFLOW_STATES.md). Do not invent a new status just to describe a particular game-engine task. ### The permission rule Research and Design may update permitted project-brain/sprint-planning Markdown; **they do not change game code, tests, assets, manifests or deployments**. Develop may alter only explicitly approved paths and commands after Gate I. A “Refine” stage does not waive this: code corrections still require valid Develop authorization. The three gates are not interchangeable: - Gate D: meaningful game design direction; - Gate I: exact implementation plan revision; - Gate A: first-hand human evaluation. ### A complete example A user wants a tiny obstacle-dodging game. Research checks whether immediate controls and simple collision are feasible in a browser. Design narrows to one duck, one obstacle type and a restart, with `AC-01` to `AC-03`. The human selects immediate movement (Gate D). The agent proposes three source files, a unit test and an authorized Node command; the human approves that exact plan (Gate I). Implementation yields a runnable arena and test results. The human reports the red obstacle is too hard to notice, so refinement investigates color contrast and proposes an in-scope change or revised plan. The user finally retests and gives Gate A. If tests pass but the user hasn't played, the proper status is `awaiting_acceptance`, **not** `accepted`. ### Common failures **Stage drift:** The agent starts coding while `STATE.md` still says `designing` with no Gate I. Stop and reconcile. **Automatic acceptance:** The coding agent marks the sprint complete because CI passed. Request actual user review. **New feature as “refinement”:** A gameplay change creates a new system beyond the approved scope. Return to Design or backlog instead. ### Related [Research](#wiki-lifecycle--research) · [Design](#wiki-lifecycle--design) · [Implement](#wiki-lifecycle--implement) · [Refine](#wiki-lifecycle--refine) · [Acceptance](#wiki-lifecycle--acceptance)

title: Stage 1 — Research
body: ## Stage 1 — Research Research is a focused investigation of uncertainty that could change the next game-design or engineering decision. It is **not** permission to begin an unbounded technical implementation. ### When to use Use Research when the idea is vague, a control model is unclear, a target engine/API may be unsupported, a performance constraint matters or a playtest exposed an unknown. ### Inputs and source discipline Start with the safe project brain and the current question: `GAME.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, optional current `SPRINT.md`, the project's permitted source and actual documentation. For each meaningful factual finding, record: - **Question:** What would change our decision? - **Evidence:** A specific source URL, repository artifact, versioned documentation or actual measurement. - **Confidence:** Verified, inferred, proposed or unknown. - **Tradeoff:** How the evidence affects player experience, scope or complexity. - **Next action:** Choice, focused experiment, or known blocker. No source? Say *not verified* and describe how to check; don't fabricate benchmark numbers, platform support or citations. ### Research should be bounded Ask whether the uncertainty can be resolved before committing to a sprint. One example: “Can keyboard and touch inputs drive the same movement function in a simple browser prototype?” This can be answered with documentation or a **read-only** code inspection. If answering requires a new runtime script, package installation or experiment that edits game files, write a plan and obtain Gate I first. A **formal research-spike sprint** still uses `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md`, `REVIEW.md`, and its Gate I is scoped to the actual research operations, even when no source code is authorized. Pre-sprint read-only discovery doesn't need a fictional Gate I. ### Outputs Focus important findings in `SPRINT.md` under Research and evidence when the sprint exists. Project-wide unknowns may be summarized in `STATE.md` or the backlog. A separate `research/` folder is optional when material no longer fits a sprint. Present the person with **two or three feasible alternatives when genuine choices exist**, a reasoned recommendation and one consequential question. ### Example: movement model The agent compares: - **Direct velocity:** immediate response, simple to test, possible abrupt feel; - **Acceleration:** nuanced feel, requires tuning and more careful testing. It might recommend direct movement for Sprint 001 because the first experiment is about obstacle legibility rather than motion physics. That recommendation is still **proposed**, not human-approved. If the user says “I'm undecided,” offer a reversible pair of trials only after describing their file scope and obtaining authorization for any code. ### Exit criteria Research is ready to advance when the problem and main unknown are clear, evidence/uncertainty is labeled, significant alternatives are visible and a meaningful decision or testable hypothesis can be proposed. It is not necessary to know every implementation detail. ### Common failures **Research rabbit hole:** Reading fifty tutorials without narrowing a decision. Stop at the first material uncertainty. **Assumption laundering:** “The engine supports this” without version/source. Mark unknown. **Research bypass:** Running an unapproved install command because “it's only a spike.” Plan actual side effects first. ### Related [Guided discovery](#wiki-learning--guided-discovery) · [Design](#wiki-lifecycle--design) · [Security](#wiki-quality--security)

title: Stage 2 — Design and Ideation
body: ## Stage 2 — Design and Ideation Design turns possibilities into **one bounded, testable gameplay outcome**. The agent facilitates and documents; the human owns material creative direction. ### When to use Use once there is enough context to propose an observable action, game-system response and acceptance test—or when a failed prototype reveals that the intended experience needs to change. ### Design brief for one slice A useful sprint brief answers: 1. **Player verb:** What does a player do? 2. **System response:** What happens in the game? 3. **Feeling or insight:** What should the player perceive or learn? 4. **Scope in/out:** What precisely isn't being built yet? 5. **Learning checkpoint:** Which mechanic/system tradeoff deserves explanation and a prediction? 6. **Acceptance criteria:** Which observable checks will determine whether the slice works? If no significant design fork exists, document `gate_d_status: not_required` with a specific reason. Do not invent a second option to create artificial approval paperwork. ### Design alternatives and Gate D A consequential choice deserves two genuine alternatives and tradeoffs. Examples: - Movement is **instant** or **inertial**; - Enemy reaction is **line-of-sight chase** or **proximity trigger**; - Level learning happens in a **safe introduction** or a **high-pressure first encounter**. Show the recommendation as advice, not a committed decision. Record the user's actual choice in `DECISIONS.md` and `SPRINT.md`, with rationale and conditions. A design approval **does not** permit writing code. ### Create the sprint pack at the right time Only after a real milestone is selected should the agent copy `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md`, and `REVIEW.md` templates into `planning/sprints/sprint-NNN/`. The agent can fill planning documents without user having to type entire schemas. `SPRINT.md` defines the intended behavior and actual `AC-##` entries **before source implementation**. Each criterion specifies test method, setup/input, observable pass condition, evidence to capture and whether it blocks release. ### Example: a dodge prototype The human approves a 2D browser slice: - move a duck in four directions; - avoid one type of moving obstacle; - hit ends the attempt, restart begins again. **Out of scope:** sounds, scoring service, level editor, multiplayer, art generator. **Learning checkpoint:** predicted difference between instantaneous and accelerating movement. `AC-01` tests input response and arena bounds. `AC-02` tests collision/game-over visibility. `AC-03` tests restart. The person should still judge actual readability and feel during later acceptance. ### Exit criteria The design stage is ready for technical planning when selected scope, player behavior, significant choices, risk assumptions and criteria are explicit. The agent then drafts `PLAN.md` and seeks **Gate I** separately. Do not allow “we agree on the game” to stand in for authorization of unreviewed paths or downloads. ### Common failures **Large invisible requirement:** “Create a fun game.” Specify what the player can do and observe. **Design by agent default:** Select platform or art style without acknowledging the user didn't choose. **Acceptance after implementation:** Define `AC-##` only when code is done. Reverse the order and obtain meaningful pre-implementation checks. ### Related [Sprint planning](#wiki-sprints--planning) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals) · [Learning checkpoints](#wiki-learning--checkpoints)

title: Stage 3 — Implement
body: ## Stage 3 — Implement Implementation is the **only stage that may actually change game source, tests, scenes, assets or dependencies**, and only while a specific **Gate I** authorization is valid. ### When to use Use when the human has reviewed the exact current `PLAN.md` revision and expressly permitted its operations. Do not invoke implementation simply because design looks ready, the shell works or a previous chat says “continue.” ### Preconditions Read `SECURITY.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `STATE.md`, the active `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md`, and relevant decisions. Verify: - active `sprint-NNN` and selected `AC-##`; - Gate D for meaningful design (or justified not-required); - plan file revision, exact operations, dependencies and commands; - **real human approval** of that same revision and scope, with conditions; - current worktree/source baseline and conflicting human changes; - special approval for destructive, paid, sensitive, public or other external effects. Missing proof means **stop**, not reinterpret the plan as authorized. ### Execution sequence 1. Inspect only the approved files and environment; check whether original assumptions still hold. 2. Implement the **smallest change** supporting one acceptance criterion. 3. Execute only approved test/build commands in their specified working directories. 4. Log actual changed paths, command outcomes, failures, versions when known and unexpected behavior. 5. Compare the diff with the approved operation list. Do not assume a green build implies no unauthorized change. 6. Fill the technical sections of `REVIEW.md`; keep human-playtest items `not_tested`. 7. Set an accurate status such as `refining` (defect) or `awaiting_acceptance` (ready for human), consistent with the state machine. ### Scope change = new approval A newly needed input package, extra script, third-party asset, credential, command, release endpoint or significantly changed gameplay behavior **invalidates** the old Gate I. Stop and present: - what changed and why; - exact new paths/commands/dependencies and risks; - revised `PLAN.md` `rN+1`; - rollback/protective handling of partial work; - explicit new authorization question. Old approval evidence remains in history; it must not be silently rewritten to cover the new scope. Minor fixes **within** the exact approved envelope need not generate repeated gates. ### Example: a fourth source file Gate I permitted `game.js`, `index.html`, `style.css` and one test file. The agent discovers it needs `audio.js` to add collision feedback. If the agreed outcome can be met with visual feedback in the approved files, use that within scope. If not, stop, explain why `audio.js` is necessary, update the plan and ask for new Gate I. Never quietly create it because it's a “small file.” ### If execution tools are unavailable Produce proposed edits/commands clearly marked as **not run** and ask the user to perform the verified steps or connect appropriate tooling. Do not claim to have executed a build, produced a local binary or inspected a browser when no such tool result exists. ### Common failures **Tool permission as consent:** The coding agent has write access to the repository, so it thinks it may modify all files. Gate I is narrower. **Silent dependency change:** A package manager upgrades versions while installing. Stop and reconcile any material difference. **Self-acceptance:** Implementation records tests as passed and closes the sprint. Gate A remains human. ### Related [Technical plan](#wiki-sprints--planning) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals) · [Testing](#wiki-quality--testing)

title: Stage 4 — Refine
body: ## Stage 4 — Refine Refinement applies **evidence from tests and human playtesting** to correct a bounded gameplay slice. It is not permission to expand the feature or edit source outside the approved technical plan. ### When to use Use after a build fails, an acceptance criterion is unmet, a player reports confusing feedback or the first prototype reveals an incorrect design hypothesis. ### The diagnosis loop 1. **Observation:** What exactly failed? Quote a real test or user's first-hand report; do not invent it. 2. **Reproduction:** What input, build, browser/device, sequence and expected behavior are known? 3. **Classification:** Is it a verified bug inside current scope, a hypothesis requiring investigation, or a new requirement/design choice? 4. **Permission:** Does existing Gate I still authorize the paths, commands, packages and risk necessary to fix it? 5. **Correction:** If in scope, make the smallest change and run approved checks. If out of scope, revise `PLAN.md` and request new Gate I. 6. **Preserve history:** Record `round-N` in `REVIEW.md`, old observations, correction, evidence and next human retest. 7. **Reassess:** Present updated test results and invite actual human evaluation. A changed *design* may require returning to Gate D before another Gate I. ### Three categories of change | Classification | Example | Correct action | | --- | --- | --- | | **In scope** | Approved movement code has an off-by-one boundary bug | Correct within valid Gate I, test, log | | **Scope expansion** | Requires a new collision library not in the plan | Stop, revise plan and seek Gate I | | **New design decision** | Player now wants a dash mechanic instead of only movement | Record/design choice, update acceptance checks, then new plan approval | **Never** label an entire second game system “just polish.” ### Example: unreadable hazard The player says: “I cannot tell that the red block is dangerous until I hit it.” The agent should record this as a human observation and investigate contrast, size, motion cues or onboarding. A revised border or shape within already approved CSS/canvas scope may be an in-scope refinement; adding sound assets, packages or a tutorial overlay beyond the plan may need new approval. A learning checkpoint can ask whether the user expected color alone to be enough, then compare the next retest with that prediction. This is meaningful education, not an artificial quiz. ### Rejection is not erasure If the user rejects a playtest, keep the original verdict, failing criteria and feedback in `REVIEW.md`. Later `round-2` can contain a new, specific result. Do not backdate or overwrite `round-1` to make the history appear continuously successful. ### Exit criteria The refined outcome is ready for human Acceptance only when it is actually runnable/inspectable, technical checks and known defects are reported accurately, and the human has concise steps aligned with the original criteria. ### Common failures **AI reacts to criticism by redesigning the entire game:** Ask which experience needs to change; keep out-of-scope ideas in backlog. **Partial approval forgotten:** The human authorized code but not new audio assets. Keep that boundary. **Fake retest:** “It should work now” is prediction, not evidence. Run actual checks or label unverified. ### Related [Human acceptance](#wiki-lifecycle--acceptance) · [Review records](#wiki-sprints--review) · [Failure recovery](#wiki-quality--failure-recovery)

title: Stage 5 — Human Acceptance
body: ## Stage 5 — Human Acceptance Acceptance evaluates **the actual player experience**. An agent can prepare tests, evidence and play instructions; only the human can supply the final verdict. ### When to use Use after an implementation or refinement cycle has an inspectable/runnable outcome, or when deciding whether a research spike answered its question. ### Prepare a fair review `REVIEW.md` should contain: - the original `AC-##` criteria from `SPRINT.md`; - commands actually run, test outcomes and device/environment where known; - a runnable build or an honest blocker; - short human test steps and expected observations; - known defects, assumptions, accessibility/device limits and release blockers; - empty Gate A verdict fields until the human responds. An agent may pass its unit tests but fail to create a usable build. Don't pretend the human could play the game if there is no actual artifact. ### Playtest the experience For a movement-and-obstacle sprint, ask the person to: 1. launch the game with the verified instructions; 2. move in each direction and test boundary collisions; 3. avoid and intentionally hit obstacles; 4. restart and observe response; 5. describe whether control feel and hazard readability matched expectations. The person's answer can be concise: “Input feels instant, but I can't see the hazard against the background.” That is more informative than a fabricated “all good.” ### Record Gate A Allowed verdicts: - **accepted** — criteria meet the human's expectations; - **accepted_with_conditions** — accepted subject to explicitly preserved conditions; - **needs_refinement** — correct and retest; - **rejected** — preserve reason and decide whether to revise or abandon; - **paused** — insufficient evidence or external blocker. Record the actual response and source in `REVIEW.md`. Conditional acceptance **with unresolved release-blocking conditions** is not unconditional completed/releasable status. The framework's documented Stage 6 validator may recognize internally consistent entries, but it **cannot authenticate human consent or gameplay experience**. A human verdict is not replaceable by code. ### Closing the sprint After genuine acceptance, update `STATE.md` and `planning/BACKLOG.md` to show what is done, what remains deferred, what was learned and the next possible slice. Preserve prior refinement rounds and past human feedback. Do **not** auto-create Sprint 002 simply because Sprint 001 closed. The person chooses the next direction. ### Research-only acceptance A formal research-spike sprint may have criteria such as “the test produced reproducible measurements” and “we can choose between two approaches.” Human Gate A evaluates whether those *evidence deliverables* answer the agreed question—not whether an imaginary game was playable. ### Common failures **Test success equals approval:** CI is green but user hasn't tried it. Keep `awaiting_acceptance`. **No evidence per criterion:** A broad “done” lacks test coverage. Map each original AC to pass/fail/partial/not-tested. **Silencing negative feedback:** An earlier rejection is removed after fixes. Preserve round history. ### Related [Playtesting](#wiki-quality--playtesting) · [Sprint review](#wiki-sprints--review) · [Refinement](#wiki-lifecycle--refine)

title: The Three-File Sprint Pack
body: ## The Three-File Sprint Pack A sprint is a **bounded experiment or playable increment** with a testable end. Light consolidates original ADDF's numerous sprint artifacts into `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md`, and `REVIEW.md` without deleting their responsibilities. ### When to use Read when creating Sprint 001, teaching a student how to plan gameplay, or evaluating whether a sprint can be safely continued after an interruption. ### The minimum pack ```text planning/sprints/sprint-001/ ├── SPRINT.md # what, why, tradeoffs, AC-##, Gate D ├── PLAN.md # how exactly, commands, dependencies, Gate I, execution └── REVIEW.md # actual results, human playtest, refinement, Gate A ``` The **blank project** does not contain a sprint folder. The agent copies the three distribution templates only after the human selects a milestone; it updates IDs/revisions to match `STATE.md` and `GAME.md`. ### Responsibilities don't merge `SPRINT.md` owns **experience intent**. It records why the sprint matters, evidence, design alternatives, learning checkpoint, in/out scope, selected direction, and `AC-##` criteria. Gate D belongs here and in significant `D-###` decisions. `PLAN.md` owns **execution scope**. It enumerates exact create/modify/move/delete paths, commands and working directories, dependencies/assets with provenance, side effects, rollback and verification. Gate I belongs here. The agent's actual command results also live here. `REVIEW.md` owns **evidence and verdicts**. Every acceptance criterion has a real result or `not_tested`. Human observations and each refinement round remain visible. Gate A belongs here, never in a model's unverified confidence. ### A good first sprint A tiny dodge game could test: - AC-01: four-direction control with arena bounds; - AC-02: one repeating hazard clearly triggers failure; - AC-03: restart resets the attempt. It would exclude high-score services, audio, art-generation pipelines, multiplayer and future levels until needed. This makes a playable and inspectable outcome likely within one iteration. ### The sprint lifecycle 1. Choose one backlog candidate or focused question. 2. Research and design its player outcome; draft `SPRINT.md`. 3. Obtain Gate D for meaningful choices. 4. Draft the exact `PLAN.md` dry run; obtain Gate I. 5. Implement and test inside authorized scope, recording actual evidence. 6. Refine if tests or players expose defects, re-authorizing new scope. 7. Provide a runnable artifact and ask for human Gate A. 8. Preserve the verdict, retrospective and handoff; choose the next sprint later. A formal no-code research-spike sprint still documents its bounded plan and evidence even though it authorizes **no game code**. ### Common failures **Premature sprint folder:** The framework creates ten empty sprints at initialization. Keep only the active selected sprint. **Approval conflation:** Design choice is treated as permission for commands. Split D and I. **Missing history:** A correction erases an earlier negative playtest. Preserve review rounds. ### Related [Planning](#wiki-sprints--planning) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals) · [Review and retrospective](#wiki-sprints--review) · [File reference](#wiki-reference--file-reference)

title: Backlog: Keep Ideas Without Building Them Yet
body: ## Backlog: Keep Ideas Without Building Them Yet The backlog collects possible player outcomes, research experiments and deferred work. Its purpose is to **protect focus** while preserving future ideas. ### When to use Use when a brainstorming session produces too many ideas, when playtesting suggests a new feature, or when a designer asks why a requested system isn't in the active sprint. ### One item = observable outcome Each candidate uses a stable `B-###` ID and records title, player-facing outcome, priority, status, dependency, linked sprint (if any) and rationale. For example: ```md ### B-003 — Clear hazard feedback - id: B-003 - title: Clear hazard feedback - outcome: A first-time player can identify hazards before colliding. - priority: next - status: candidate - depends_on: B-001 - sprint: none - reason: Playtest feedback suggests the first obstacle is hard to perceive. ``` Do not interpret the example as a real entry until the human actually requests or confirms it. ### Selecting a first slice A meaningful `priority: now` candidate should be small enough to answer one question. If “Build enemy AI” contains movement, animation, targeting, health and coordination, split it into separate outcomes. The user chooses consequential priorities; the agent may recommend ordering based on evidence and dependencies. Only after selection should an item become `status: selected` and link to a real `sprint-NNN`. Backlog inclusion does not authorize implementation. ### Research spikes versus features A research spike might ask: “Can this browser build reliably access the needed controller inputs?” Its deliverable is sourced evidence or a deliberately authorized experiment, **not** a full input system. Label its outcome explicitly to avoid presenting research progress as shipped gameplay. ### Updates after playtesting After the human's Gate A verdict, the agent can mark the completed slice, defer new suggestions, preserve discarded ideas with reasons, and recommend the next candidate. “Needs refinement” may stay inside the current sprint if the fix is within scope or requires a revised authorization. Stable IDs aren't recycled when an idea is rejected. Status values include `candidate`, `selected`, `in-progress`, `completed`, `deferred` and `discarded`. ### Example prioritization A designer wants enemy waves, new art and more levels. The last test showed movement controls are inconsistent. The agent recommends fixing controls **before** enemy waves because later difficulty feedback will be unreliable otherwise. The user can disagree; the choice and reasoning should be recorded if material. ### Common failures **Backlog as permission:** The agent implements a “next” idea without a sprint and Gate I. Stop. **Infinite backlog grooming:** The team spends more time ranking ideas than testing them. Prioritize only enough to select the next slice. **Deletion without reasoning:** Rejected ideas disappear. Preserve status and reason. ### Related [Sprint overview](#wiki-sprints--overview) · [Decisions](#wiki-learning--decisions) · [Scope and planning](#wiki-sprints--planning)

title: Planning and the Exact Dry Run
body: ## Planning and the Exact Dry Run `PLAN.md` is the boundary between thoughtful design and implementation permission. Its function is not to produce a long essay; it's to make the **real edits and effects visible to the human before they occur**. ### When to use Use after a bounded sprint and its acceptance checks are selected, before any game-source, test, asset, manifest or deployment configuration is edited. ### First check the inputs Verify the active sprint ID, `SPRINT.md` revision, selected design and Gate D evidence. Check the actual repository and known files **read-only** within `SECURITY.md` boundaries. A missing dependency or unknown engine installation should be reported, not guessed. ### Fill the plan The required dry run covers: | Section | Practical question | | --- | --- | | Inputs/assumptions | Which approved sprint revision and project state are we planning for? | | Exact file operations | What exact files are created, modified, moved or deleted, and why? | | Commands/side effects | What commands run, where, and what do they write/download? | | Dependencies/assets | Which versions, licenses, downloads and outside services are involved? | | Implementation sequence | What's the smallest safe sequence? | | Verification plan | How will each `AC-##` be tested, and who tests player feel? | | Risks/rollback | What might break, what should stop work and how is it reversed? | | Open ambiguities | Which unresolved questions prevent authorization? | | Gate I | What exact revision/scope did the human approve? | | Execution record | What actually happened after authorization? | ### Example dry-run scope ```md | Operation | Exact path | Purpose | Scope constraint | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | create | game.js | AC-01 movement | No networking or inventory | | create | index.html | Playable arena | One page, no external embeds | | create | tests/game.test.cjs | AC-01/02 logic | Existing Node test runner only | ``` The command section might authorize `node --test tests/game.test.cjs` in the game folder and **no package installation**. Any necessary additional command must appear in a revised plan. A broad wildcard such as “all files needed” is not a suitable authorized scope. ### Ask for a precise Gate I After showing the plan, ask: “Do you authorize Sprint 001 `PLAN.md` r1 for these paths and commands, with these exclusions?” Record the **actual reply** and its source. A user may approve only a subset; revise the plan to accurately reflect that rather than stretching the words. Plan revision `r2` that adds a dependency or a file **requires fresh Gate I**. Preserve earlier revision/approval history; never overwrite it to imply retroactive consent. ### Approvals and technical capability An agent tool with shell access can technically run a command even before permission exists. That doesn't make it authorized. A validator that sees `gate_i_status: authorized` may check matching fields but cannot verify the human actually typed the response. Public deployment, purchases, secret access, destructive operations or external messages require **separate explicit special approval**, not just ordinary coding Gate I. ### Common failures **Plan without acceptance checks:** How can a reviewer judge whether files are necessary? Define `AC-##` first. **Version mismatch:** Gate I says r1, current plan says r2. Stop and re-approve. **Execution before authorization:** An agent runs npm install “just to inspect.” Treat the install as a side effect needing review. ### Related [Approvals](#wiki-sprints--approvals) · [Implement stage](#wiki-lifecycle--implement) · [Security](#wiki-quality--security)

title: Human Approval Gates: D, I and A
body: ## Human Approval Gates: D, I and A Light's three gates intentionally distribute authority across **experience**, **execution**, and **evaluation**. Skipping one cannot be compensated for by extra technical tests. ### When to use Use when the user asks “Can the agent just continue?”, when scope changes, or when an AI marks work complete without first-hand verification. ### Gate D — Significant design choices Gate D settles consequential player experience, scope, architecture or technology direction. The agent offers genuine alternatives, tradeoffs, evidence and a recommendation, then asks one direct question. Record actual choice in `DECISIONS.md` and the sprint's `SPRINT.md`. No material design fork? A justified `not_required` may be acceptable. A trivial variable name inside existing approved behavior need not trigger a full design vote. **Gate D never authorizes code edits.** ### Gate I — Exact implementation authorization The agent presents `PLAN.md` before code changes. The reviewer sees: - current revision and linked sprint; - exact create/modify/move/delete paths; - shell commands, directories, side effects and external service access; - dependency versions, downloads/asset provenance; - security, destructive or paid actions; - test strategy, risks, rollback and exclusions. Only clear permission for this **exact** scope allows Develop to act. Ambiguous “go ahead” about a concept is insufficient if the file/command plan wasn't shown. **Gate I becomes stale** when files, commands, dependency/version, material behavior, risk or external effects change. The agent stops, documents the difference and requests a new gate for the revised plan. ### Gate A — Human acceptance The agent presents the runnable artifact, actual tests, failing/untested checks and short playtest steps. The human evaluates and provides a verdict: `accepted`, `accepted_with_conditions`, `needs_refinement`, `rejected`, or `paused`. Automated tests can establish logical behavior but cannot decide whether the mechanic feels responsive, a level is readable or an onboarding interaction makes sense. A condition that blocks release must remain a blocker even if the human conditionally approves the sprint. ### Approval records Each gate has a source/revision reference and recorded human wording or durable review link. Agents may transcribe actual approvals, **never invent them**. A model's memory or generated checkbox does not independently prove consent. Gate location: - D: `SPRINT.md`, cross-linked to `D-###`; - I: `PLAN.md`, reflected in `STATE.md`; - A: `REVIEW.md`, reflected in `STATE.md`. ### A common ambiguity The human says, “Yes, I like the dodge game.” This may settle a concept preference, not authorization to create files or install Phaser. The agent should acknowledge the selected direction, show the technical plan, and ask: “Do you authorize r1's exact operations?” After implementation, “The tests all pass” isn't an acceptance verdict. Ask the human to try the game and describe whether the agreed experience works. ### Stop conditions When an approval can't be verified, degrade to a **safe non-implementation state**. Do not forge the missing record or proceed because a previous agent claimed it was approved. ### Common failures **Gate bundling by inference:** Treat enthusiasm as all three gates. Split the records. **Retroactive consent:** Add new paths to r1 after its approval. Create r2 and ask again. **AI self-acceptance:** The agent fills “human verdict: accepted.” Keep pending until real review. ### Related [Normative approval policy](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/APPROVAL_POLICY.md) · [Plan](#wiki-sprints--planning) · [Review](#wiki-sprints--review)
